Action against Al officials 
*302. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  two Air India traffic officers 
were intercepted at the Heathrow Airport at London in early June, 2005 with 
contraband items from India and deport ed back to Mumbai on account of 
their failure to pay up the fine/penalty imposed by the UK Customs; 
(b) whether AI has taken appropriate disciplinary action against the 
errant officials; and 
(c) whether Government will ensure that the crew of our flag carriers 
flying to overseas destinations are constantly drilled to keep away from such 
unlawful activities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL 
AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to  (c) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Disciplinary action as per the provisions of the Certified Standing 
Orders is being initiated by Air India Management against the two 
employees. 
 
1

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
(c) Yes, Sir. Air India Management issues circulars from time to time 
drawing the attention of the employees, particularly the crew, that they should 
strictly follow the customs regulations and any violation of these rules would 
attract severe punishment. Moreover, the following regulations/orders are in 
force to deal with the errant officials: 
(i) Air India Employees Regulations, which is applicable to officers & 
executives, has clauses under misconduct, which relates to breach of 
Customs Act, FERA, Narcotics Act etc. as well as smuggling, aiding 
or carrying of goods with object of pecuniary gain. 
(ii) Certified Standing Orders which is applicable to workmen categories 
of staff has clauses under misconduct, which relate to conviction is 
court of law for any criminal offence as well as smuggling, aiding or 
carrying goods with object of pecuniary gain. 
PROF. P.J. KURIAN: Sir, question number 301 is a very important 
question. ...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Sir, two Air India Traffic Officers were 
deported from the Heathrow Airport, London, allegedly for attempting to 
smuggle 8,400 cartoons of Indian cigare ttes worth about Rs. 35,000. It may 
not be a big amount. But, Sir, the crew of the carriers flying overseas 
destinations enjoy a certain measure of immunity in formal life. While they 
arrive home, the Indian Custom office ta kes a lenient view of their baggage. 
Sir, taking advantage of this leniency, there have been instances where Indian 
Airlines and Air India staff were involved in bringing countermand small, 
personal lots and personal baggage, i would like to know from the hon. 
Minister, whether Air India has in place any in-house vigilance mechanism to 
check on-board delinquency by its officers. 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, the ho n. Member has mentioned about 
these two cases which happened in London. Just for his information, action 
will be taken against them. It happened in June.and the U.K. Custom 
Department is sending us the formal documents. However, with regard to the 
other issues, specially about the crew coming into India, in the last two years 
alone, 14 cases have been registered concerning cabin crew for bringing 
things beyond their permissible limits. In seven cases, people have been 
punished, and in the balance cases, departmental action is in 
2 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
progress. On the other issue of what is the system and mechanism about 
detecting cases of some theft or other issues on board, Sir, Air India has an 
on-board surveillance programme. Some vigilance people are sent on-board, 
from time to time, and, at the end of the flight, these vigilance people do try 
to take stock of the goods on board whether they have been accounted for and 
are in a prescribed manner. Some cases  have been found and action has been 
taken from time to time. 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Sir, in my second supplementary I would 
like to know from the Minister whether Air India and Indian Airlines have, in 
their service or employment contract, any provision for summary dismissal of 
the staff from service, if any crew or staff is found guilty in custom violation 
cases. 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL Sir I am sure, action leading to dismissal also 
would be a part of the procedure. But, in the interest of natural justice and the 
prescribed procedure, inquiry and other things are conducted, from time to 
time, in the prescribed manner. And, if  action is warranting a dismissal, even 
that has been taken; and that has been taken in the past in many cases. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. It is a 
question of mindset of these crew members. Does the Government plan to 
change their mindset, because they thin k they can get away with anything? 
So, unless we take some definite steps, not only disciplinary, but under 
different Acts also, this mindset will not change. That is one thing. 
Simultaneously, Sir, there is a wrong information. I think, the word 'FERA 
has been written. FERA is no more any law in the country. I would like to tell 
the Minister and his office that there is no FERA in the country anymore. So, 
where is the scope of FERA? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, I ap preciate the concern of the hon. 
Member that we should improve the mindset; we should condition them to be 
more vigilant, more loyal to the airline, and to the company for which they 
work. However, all these exercises also in a way are deterrent for them to do 
not do these things. But your point is well taken. I will also convey your 
sentiments to the management of Air India that they should try to inculcate in 
them a sense of belonging to the airline, and to the country, of course. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
On the issue of FERA, Sir, there may have been cases of FERA 
registered in the past when FERA was applicable; maybe some cases here 
reflecting an earlier action which may have been contemplated under FERA. 
But your point is again well taken. Now, there is FEMA instead of FERA. So, 
in future, I hope, there will be no such cases. Your concern that there may be 
such cases, I only pray to God that th ere should not be any more FEMA cases 
in future. 
Post closure adjustment on sale of PSUs 
*303 SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHER JEE: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred Question 1616 given in 
the Rajya Sabha on the 16th March, 2003 and state the details of post closure 
adjustments, made in the case of BALCO, Paradeep Phosphates, HTL, Jessop, 
ITDC Hotels, Airport Hotels, IPCL, VSNL and other cases of strategic sale of 
PSUs? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Post disinvestment matters are handled by the concerned administrative 
ministries/departments. Details of post closure adjustment in individual cases 
of disinvestment through strategic sale are given below. 
Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd. (BALCO): The post closure 
adjustment is under consideration of the Ministry of Mines. 
Paradeep Phosphates Ltd. (PPL): The post closure adjustment is under 
consideration of the Department of Fertilizers. 
HTL Ltd.: The post closure adjustment is being dealt by the Department 
of Telecommunications. In accordance  with the prov isions of the 
Shareholders' Agreement, the strategic partner invoked the arbitration clause 
and the matter is already before an Arbitral Panel. 
India Tourism Development Corporation Ltd. (ITDC): A statement 
indicating the position of post closure adjustment in 19 disinvested hotels of 
ITDC is at Statement I (See below). 
Hotel Corporation of India Ltd. (HCI): Post closure adjustment has 
been completed in respect of Indo Hokke Hotels Limited, a subsidiary 
4 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of HCI. The purchaser has been paid an amount of Rs. 4.33 lakh in settlement 
of the preferred claim. In the case of  Centaur Hotel Airport, Mumbai, the 
matter is under arbitration. In the case of Centaur Hotel Juhu Beach, Mumbai, 
the post closure adjustments have not been concluded. The parties have 
mutually agreed to refer the matter to the Ministry of Civil Aviation for 
adjudication. 
Modern Food Industries (India) Ltd. (MFIL): The post closure auditors 
determined an amount of Rs. 23.62 crore as the decrease in net current assets 
between the reference date and the closing date. Based on this, M/s Hindustan 
Lever Ltd (HLL) claimed Rs. 17.48 crore (74 percent of Rs. 23.62 crore) 
towards post closure adjustment. After scrutiny of the claim, Rs. 12.64 crore 
has been paid to HLL. However, HLL still claims Rs. 4.43 crore under post 
closure adjustment, which is under examination of the Ministry of Food 
Processing Industries. 
No provision for post closure adjustment exists in the disinvestment 
cases of Lagan Jute Machinery Compan y Ltd, CMC Ltd., IBP Ltd., Videsh 
Sanchar Nigam Ltd, Hindustan Zinc Ltd, Indian Petrochemical Corporation 
Ltd, Maruti Udyog Ltd and Jessop & Company Ltd.

Non-payment of mediclaim by insurance companies 
†*304. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have r eceived complaints regarding non-
payment of mediclaim by the health insurance companies; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
8 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by Government in this regard; and 
(c) whether some companies have given suggestions for its 
improvement? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM) (a): to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. Government have received complaints regarding non-
payment of mediclaim by the General Insurance Companies. 
(b) and (c) The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority 
(IRDA) has been established as an independent regulator. Its objective inter 
alia, is to protect the interest of the policyholders. IRDA has notified the 
Insurance and Development Authority (Protection of Policyholders, Interest) 
Regulations, 2002. These Regulations stipulate the duties and obligations of 
the insurers and policyholders in respect of an insurance contract, both at the 
point of sale and in the event of a claim, and setting up of in-house grievance 
redressal mechanism in the insurance companies. In pursuance of these 
regulations, the companies have set up in-house grievance redressal 
mechanisms, which are refined from time to time on the basis of feedback 
received by them. In addition to this, fo r grievances relating to settlement of 
claims, policyholders also approach the Government, Insurance Ombudsmen, 
IRDA Grievance Cell, Consumer Fora and the courts. Government on receipt 
of such grievances sends them to insurance companies/Ombudsmen for 
redressal.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the total complaints received by or 
against non-life companies by the ombudsmen is a small proportion of the 
total claims which are received and which are settled, I think, one has to look 
at it in perspective. For example, in 2C04-05, in respect of medi-claim 
policies, that is, medical insurance policies, the number of claims received by 
the four public sector companies by people who had paid for medical 
treatment and, therefore, claiming insurance benefit, was 6,62,815 received in 
that year. The number of claims settled — current claims as well as claims 
made in the earlier years-was 6,73,661. Therefore, the bulk of the claims are 
usually settled. A complaint arises, Sir, when a claim is not settled; when the 
insurance company's answer is disput ed by the insurer. That is when it 
becomes a complaint. The complaints are, as I said, a small number. For 
example, in 2003-04, the ombudsmen r eceived, in all non- life claims against 
the four public sector insurance companies only 5707 complaints; out of 
which, 3528 have been disposed of. Disposal ratio is about 61 per cent. There 
are three levels of complaints redressal—one at the company level, one at the 
ombudsmen level and the last, at the IRDA level. Hon Member is right that 
Government also received some comp laints. But the Government cannot 
become another level of complaints redressal. So, what we do is that, we 
forward the complaint, either to the IRDA's Complaint Redressal Cell or to 
the Ombudsman. They take over the complaints and redress these complaints. 
I think, the complaints are small in number, and they are being handled. But, 
I think, we need to have proper documentation of the complaints. I have

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, VAT is a State tax. VAT is intended 
to replace the erstwhile Sales Tax, which is a law of the State under Entry-54 
of Lisf-ll of the Seventh Schedule. The Government of India's role is that of a 
facilitator. It is the States in a meeting and in a formally constituted 
Empowered Committee which have voluntarily and willingly adopted VAT 
to replace Sales Tax because we believe, and most people believe, that it is a 
more efficient tax, it is a revenue enhancing tax, it is a fair and 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
transparent tax. Now, yes, Bihar is re porting in the first quarter a 13.9 per 
cent decline in VAT revenues as oppose d to the Sales Tax revenues of the 
corresponding quarter of the last fi scal. This could be because of a 
multiplicity of reasons. One of the reasons could be that some Sales Tax rates 
were much higher and the  common agreed VAT rate  on that commodity 
would be much lower and, therefore, there would indeed be a revenue loss on 
that commodity. It could also be because of the poor administration, it could 
also be because VAT Is a new law and it takes some time for the law to be 
understood, accepted and obeyed by the taxpayer. I do not think this House 
should reach any conclusions based on one quarter. We are replacing a law, 
the Sales Tax law, which if I recall right, has been in place for the last 70 
years. So, a 70 year old law is being replaced by a new law, no conclusion 
can be reached on the basis of one-quarter figures. If you look at all the 22 
States, which have adopted VAT, you will find that VAT is showing an 
increase of revenue by 15.3 per cent. I think we should give time to each 
State to administer VAT and reach some  conclusions only by the end of the 
year..(interruptions)... As far as assistance is concerned, we have provided 
some amount in the Budget for compensating the States according to a pre-
agreed formula. Once the Accountant-General reconcile figures are available, 
if there is a loss due to the administra tion of VAT rates, the Government of 
India will compensate the States 100 per cent in the first year, 75 per cent in 
the second year and 50 pe r cent in the third year. This formula is also a 
formula not imposed by me but agreed to by the State Finance Ministers.

†316.   SHRIMATI PREMACARIAPPA: 
SHRI JANARDAN DWIVEDI: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) the impact of skyrocketing oil pr ices and bountiful increase in

last two years; and

exchange reserve? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHR I P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and 
(b) Foreign exchange reserves of a country, at any given point in time, 
represent the net outcome of transactio ns in the current and capital accounts 
of the country's balance of payments. Merchandise imports (i.e. oil and non-
oil) constitute a part of current accoun t transactions. Notwithstanding the rise 
in oil and non-oil imports in recent years, India's fo reign exchange reserves 
have continued to increase due to robust growth of merchandise exports and 
buoyant invisibles and capital inflows, the overall balance of payments 
position, as reflected by the increase/ decrease in foreign exchange reserves, 
continued to be comfortable with Such reserves increasing by US$ 36.9 
billion in 2003-04 and US$ 28.6 billion in 2004-05, respectively. 
(c) The broad principles guiding India's foreign exchange reserves 
management includes a policy of maintaining a level of foreign exchange 
reserves, which takes into account no t only anticipated current account 
deficits, but also liquidity-at-risk arising from unanticipated capital 
movements. Taking these factors into  account, India's foreign exchange 
reserves continue adequate and comfortable.

(d) and (e) Excise duty exempti on for Small Scale Industries is

current pension liabilities at a whopping Rs. 1.7 trillion;

system which does not add up to pension liabilities further, the debt GDP ratio

approximately which is about 55.88% of India's GDP.

defines the liability of Government upfront in the case of Government 
employees and limits Government's liability on account of future pension 
payments, which would otherwise continue to increase if new recruits were to 
be covered under the earlier system.

Review of functioning of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
2280. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI 
RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any review of the functioning of the Panchayati Raj 
institutions, with particular reference to utilization of authorities devolved to 
the respective tiers of the institutions, vis-a-vis those envisaged in the Law, 
across the country; 
(b) if so, the salient findings thereof especially highlighting the weak-
spots and loopholes, if any, which might have been found to be hindering 
better realization of the objectives of the institutions, State-wise; and 
(c) the measures initiated, if any, to facilitate improvement of the 
prevailing situations? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Panchayati Raj convened seven Round 
Table meetings with State Ministers in charge of Panchayati Raj and evolved, 
by consensus, a set of around 150 points for action which have been put 
together in a compendium that was adopted unanimously at the conclusion of 
the last Round Table in Jaipur. A Council of State Ministers of Panchayati 
Raj under the Chairmanship of Union Minister for Panchayati Raj has been 
constituted to monitor the implementation of the recommendations. 
A Committee of Chief Secretaries of  States and State Panchayati Raj 
Secretaries has been constituted under the Chairmanship of the Secretary 
(Panchayati Raj) to monitor the progress on the implementation of the 150 
recommendations of the Seven Round "Babies. Two review 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
meetings of the Committee have so far been held on the 11th April, 2005 and 
29th June, 2005. The inaugural meeting of the Council has been held on 5th-
6th August, 2005 at Kochi. The progress in devolution of functions was 
reviewed and it was noted that while in some States, the preliminary work has 
been completed in terms of the assignment of functions to the three levels of 
panchayats, in several more, the matter is pending at the finalization stage. A 
copy of Joint Statement of conclusions arrived at the meeting is at Statement-! 
(See below). 
The Minister has now initiated a process of visiting each of the 
States/UTs to review with the authorities concerned the progress in 
implementing the points for action contained in the compendium. It is 
expected that this will accelerate the base  of implementation of provisions of 
Part IX, read with Article 243ZD of the constitutions and bring about greater 
conformity, in both letter and spirit, to the Constitutional provisions of 
Panchayati Raj in all States/UTs concerned. 
He has so far visited Karnataka, West Bengal and Uttaranchal. The 
documents issued at the conclusion of each of these visits are given at 
Statements II, III and IV respectively. 
Statement I 
Joint statement of conclusions arrived at the meeting held at Kochi on 5th 
and 6th August, 2005 
In order to operationalise the provisions of Article 243 G of the 
Constitution, which provides for devolution to empower Panchayati Raj 
Institutions (PRIs) to function as institutions of self-Government for making 
plans and implementing programmes for economic development and social 
justice the first Round Table of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj held at 
Kolkata in July 2004 resolved as follows, under  the heading, "Effective 
Devolution of Functions." 
"the essential step is the identification of activities related to the 
devolved functions with a veiw to attributing each of these activities to 
the appropriate tier of the 3-tier system;" (Item III), 
"On the basis of the identification of activities relating to devolved 
functions, and through the application of the principle of the 
subsidiarity, States/UTs may review/undejtake time bound activity 
120 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
mapping with a view to completing this exercise within the fiscal year 
2004-05;" (Item V), 
"With a view to promoting a measure of irrevocability of devolved 
functions, devolution may be routed through legislative measures or, 
alternatively, by providing a strong legislative framework for 
devolution through executive orders." (Item VIII) 
The First Meeting of the Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj 
reviewed the progress in this direction and noted that while in some States, 
the preliminary work has been completed in terms of the assignment of 
functions to the three levels of panchayats, in several more, the matter is 
pending at the finalization stage. 
However in most States, there is a need to take several more 
substantive steps in the direction of reforms for strengthening Panchayats in 
the true letter and spirit of the Constitution. To this end, State Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj reiterated their commitment to address itself the resolutions 
of the Kolkata Round Table with all de liberate speed and resolved to accord 
priority to the specific following steps: 
(i) Internal discussions with State departments will be expedited so as 
to finalise the consensus on Activity Mapping within the State. 
The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will be informed of the 
time line for completing this work. 
(ii) With respect to those areas wh ere there is a general consensus as 
to the devolution of functions and activities to all levels of 
Panchayats, States will expedite the issuing of necessary orders to 
operationalise the same. Copies of Government orders/Gazette 
Notifications will be intimated to Ministry of Panchayati Raj. 
(iii) It is desirable for States to fix milestones in Activity Mapping, and 
take preparatory steps through dissemination of draft frameworks 
prepared to the Panchayats, so that they are in a" state of 
preparedness to assume their new responsibilities. The Union 
Ministry of Panchayati Raj may be kept informed of steps being 
taken in this direction. 
(iv) Training programmes for Panchayats members should include 
special sessions on the scope and implications of Activity 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
Mapping, particularly with reference to their roles in planning 
and implementation. The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will 
extent financial and technological assistance, if asked. 
(v)  Particular emphasis will be given to training and orientation of 
officials of various line departments, so that they better 
understand their role in the changed context of devolution of 
activities to Panchayats and are better equipped to assume a 
facilitator/ role. The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will extent 
financial and technological assistance, if asked. 
(vi)  For effectively performing the functions devolved to them 
through Activity Mapping, the Panchayats would need a 
matching transfer of funds in re spect of the devolved functions. 
This will require the entrustment of all schemes pertaining to the 
activities devolved upon Panchayats to the respective levels 
through the creation of a Panchaya t Sector in the State Budget. 
The State Ministers undertakes to ta ke steps in this direction, so 
as to meet the deadline agreed upon in the Kolkata Round" Table 
to operationalise the transfer of schemes to Panchayats in the 
budget of 2006-07. The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will 
take into account progress in this  regard in the administration of 
the Panchayat Empowerment Incentive Fund after this is 
established. 
(vii) For Panchayats to effectively plan and implement the functions 
that have been devolved upon them it is necessary that funds 
pertaining to these schemes are transferred to them without delay 
or diversion. As part of this process, States need to put in place 
systems that are capable of tr acking transfers of funds to 
panchayats, both through Banks and treasuries. This would 
particularly ensure tagging tracking of releases and expenditure 
of 12th Finance Commission Grants. To this end, Union Ministry 
of Panchayati Raj will work in close association with the 
Government, to put in place the required hardware and software. 
(viii) States will furnish Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj, details of 
Activities devolved to Panchayats so as to build a national 
database in this regard, which would also be of considerable use 
in devising policies and schemes at the Central level. 
122 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The challenges in sustaining the p ace of reform will require effective 
support and close coordination with the Central Government. The Ministry of 
Panchayati Raj would continue to support and coordinate activity mapping 
and take the specific following steps: 
(i) The Ministry of Panchayati Raj will pursue the devolution of 
Central funds through united block grants, and systemic reform 
of Centrally Sponsored Schemes, including the establishment of a 
Panchayat Empowerment Incentive Fund to bring these in 
conformity with the constitutional provisions for good 
governance at the district and sub-district levels as set out in Part-
IX read with the relevant articles of Part-IXA. 
(ii) The Ministry of Panchayati Raj agrees to support initiatives in 
computerization and e-Governance of Panchayats in Uttaranchal 
as part of the National e-Governance Plan. 
(iii) The Ministry of Panchayati Raj will continue to provide technical 
         support, wherever necessary, for Activity Mapping. In addition, 
        the Ministry would also provide support for the preparation of 
          material for training programmes that would necessarily follow 
Activity Mapping in States. 
(iv)  Fact sheets furnished by States on Activity Mapping and details 
of innovations and best practices will be disseminated on the 
National Panchayat Portal.

Devolution to Panchayats in Karnataka: The way forward: 
Joint Statement of conclusions arrive d at after the visit of the Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj and Petrol eum and Natural Gas to Karnataka on 
the 29th April and 1st May, 2005: 
Karnataka has championed the noble cause of empowering Panchayats 
and devolving powers to them since decades. The State has been at the 
forefront of the empowerment of all thr ee levels of Panchayats so that they 
function as institutions of local self-Government in the letter and spirit of 
Part-IX of the Constitution. The recent measures of the Karnataka 
Government stand testimony to its sustained support to Panchayati Raj 
reform. The amendments made to the Karnataka 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
Panchayat Raj Act in October 2003 and the subsequent steps taken to 
strengthen the Grama Sabha; create an d empower Ward Sabhas; complete 
Activity Mapping; and rationalize and simplify schemes entrusted to the 
Panchayats are examples to be emulated countrywide. The monitoring of the 
actualization of devolution by the Legislative Committees is a significant step 
in the strengthening of Panchayats in the State. The entrustment of schemes 
by the State Government to Panchayats in the current year's budget is a giant 
step forward in matching the functional transfer with funds. Through this 
process, the Panchayats now handle in  excess of Rs. 3500 crores of Plan 
funds per year. However there is a n eed to both substantially increase the 
quantum of funds available at each leve l of Panchayats and to untie the bulk 
of these funds. 
A fresh national impetus has been given to the devolution of powers 
and responsibilities through the Seven Round Tables of State Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj which arrived by consensus, at 150 recommendations 
pertaining to 18 dimensions of Panchayat Raj. Karnataka has initiated 
implementation of 77 of the 106 recommendations of the Round Tables that 
pertain to it. The Government of Karnataka will address itself with all 
deliberate speed to the remaining recommendations. 
• The challenges before Karnataka in  sustaining the pace of reform 
will require effective support and close coordination with the Central 
Government. In this endeavour the State Government of Karnataka 
and the Union Ministry of Pancha yati Raj, have agreed to accord 
priority to the following points. 
• Karnataka has devolved through legislation all the 29 matters in the 
Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution to the Panchayats. This 
functional transfer has been further clarified through an Activity 
Mapping framework, issued in August 2003. This has been followed 
by the entrustment of all schemes pertaining to the activities 
devolved upon Panchayats to the respective levels, in the State 
Budget of 2005-06. In the letter and spirit of Article 243 G of the 
Constitution, the Government of Karnataka commit itself to 
following up the devolution of functions and funds with the 
matching devolution of functionaries. 
• For Panchayats to effectively plan and implement the functions that 
have been devolved upon them it is necessary that funds 
124 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
pertaining to these schemes are tran sferred to them without delay or 
diversion. Karnataka has already shown the way by putting in place 
a Bank transfer mechanism for transferring funds to Gram 
Panchayats. In continuation of this reform process, it agrees to put in 
place systems that are capable of tracking transfers of funds to 
panchayats. 
• The Government of Karnataka will consider the establishment of a 
cadre of administrative and technical staff exclusively for PRIs. 
• Karnataka has recently conducted el ections to the Gram Panchayats 
and is due to conduct elections to the Taluk and Zilla Panchayats 
shortly. A new set of elected representatives have assumed office. 
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj shall assist the Government of 
Karnataka in capacity building and training of these representatives. 
• In order to build capacity and leadership among categories for 
whom seats are reserved, Karnatak a shall consider favourably the 
slowing down of the reservation cycle so that the option to reserve 
seats for more than one-term is open but it is for the State 
Legislature to decide the number  of terms for which seats will 
remain reserved. 
• The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will pursue the devolution of 
Central funds through untied block grants, and systemic reform of 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, including the establishment of a 
Panchayat Empowerment Incentive Fund to bring these in 
conformity with the constitutional provisions for good governance at 
the district and sub-district levels as set out in Part IX read with the 
relevant articles of Part IXA.

Devolution to Panchayats in West Bengal: The way forward: 
Joint Statement of conclusions arrive d at after the visit of the Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj and Petroleum and Natural Gas to West Bengal 
on the 13th, 14th and 15th May, 2005: 
West Bengal has been at the forefront of the empowerment of 
Panchayats from 1973 onwards. In 1994, it enacted its State Panchayat 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
legislation to conform to the 73rd Amendment to Constitution, so as to 
establish Panchayats as institutions of local self-Government in the letter and 
spirit of Part IX of the Constitution. The steps taken in West Bengal to 
institutionalise peoples' participation through Panchayati Raj, stand testimony 
to its sustained commitment towards Panchayati Raj. 
A fresh national impetus has been given to the devolution of powers 
and responsibilities through the Seven Round Tables of States Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj, which arrived by consensus, at 150 recommendations 
pertaining to 18 dimensions of Panchayati Raj. West Bengal has initiated 
implementation of the recommendations of the Round Tables that apply to it. 
The Government of West Bengal is in broad agreement with these 
recommendations. 
The challenges before West Bengal in sustaining the pace of reform 
will require effective support and cl ose coordination with the Central 
Government. In this endeavour the State Government of West Bengal and the 
Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj, have agreed to accord priority to the 
following points: 
• West Bengal has devolved through legislation all the 29 matters in 
the Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution to the Panchayats. This 
functional transfer is being furthe r clarified through an Activity 
Mapping exercise, which has been completed for several matters 
such as agriculture, agriculture marketing, animal resources 
development, cottage and small scale industries, forestry, health and 
family welfare, fisheries, food and civil supplies, mass education 
extension, backward classes welfare, women and child development 
and social welfare and information and cultural affairs. In the letter 
and spirit of Article 243G of the Constitution, the Government of 
West Bengal commit itself to issuing the necessary orders for 
operationalising the activity mapping and then follow this with the 
matching devolution of funds. 
• For Panchayats to effectively plan and implement the functions that 
have been devolved upon them it is necessary that funds pertaining 
to these schemes are transferred to them without delay or diversion. 
In furtherance of reform in this direction, West Bengal has already 
put in place computerized system that is capable of tracking transfers 
of funds to panchayats on a pilot basis, which will be expanded in 
due course.

Audit 
(i) Since local bodies are now institutions of local self-government, it 
is necessary to upgrade the work  of the Director of Local Fund 
Audit (DLFA) and other similar bodies to the level required by 
Constitutional imperatives and, to this end, for DLFA and other 
similar bodies to work in concert with the Comptroller and 
Auditor General of India (C&AG). 
(ii) In recognition of PRIs being institutions of local self-government, 
PRIs themselves should be associ ated with the preparation of 
standards and norms and the emphasis should be on fund 
management and fund tracking, rather than simply on fund flow, 
to ensure greater accountability. 
(iii) In order to ensure that such audit contributes effectively to 
capping, reducing and eventually  eliminating the scope for 
corruption in Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), it is necessary 
that audit and accounting standards appropriate to the work of the 
Panchayats be established and observed. These standards should 
be elementary, simple and easily comprehensible to the elected 
representatives, and should focus on: 
- when transactions should be looked into; 
- what should be monitored; 
138 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
- how the transactions should be documented; and 
- how they should be disclosed. 
(iv) There is need to establish an in ternal audit system at every tier of 
the Panchayati Raj system and to regard C&AG audit (or audit by 
bodies certified or technically guided by C&AG) as 
complementary external audit. 
(v) Audit, to be effective, might include the establishment of a 
National Accounting Standard  Eoard (NASB) for local 
government accounts and be complemented by the establishment 
of audit commissions or similar such regulatory bodies at the 
State level. 
(vi) Besides, arrangements may be made in State Legislatures for the 
establishment of Public Accounts Committee (PACs) . specifically 
for PRIs or for the accounts of PRIs to be submitted to PR 
Committees of the State Legislatures . State level committees, as in 
Andhra Pradesh, for the settlement of audit paras may also be 
considered. 
(vii) It may be useful to complement such institutional arrangements 
by legislating an ap propriate Fiscal Reponsibility Act for elected 
local authorities. 
(viii) Outsourcing of accounting by such measures as village 
panchayats being authorized to employ certified Chartered 
Accountants against standard contracts might be considered. 
(ix) The training of both officials and elected representatives in sound 
accounting and audit practices is a high priority. To this end, 
State Governments are invited to make full use of the Regional 
Training Institutes (RTIs) functioning under the aegis of the 
C&AG, in particular the RTI at Kolkata which has been declared 
a centre of excellence; as also of the Institute of Public Auditors 
of India (IPAI). Substantial additional funding from the Union 
Government to facilitate training is a high priority. 
(x) Those State Governments which have not as yet availed of the 
arrangements for bringing the C & AG into the exercise of 
accounting and audit, including the C&AG's Technical 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
Guidance and Supervision (TGS) Scheme for the PRIs, are 
invited to do so and the attention of all concerned is drawn to the 
publications of the Indian and Audit Accounts Department, in 
particular. 
(a) Auditing Standards for PRIs and Urban Local Bodies 
(b) Guidelines for Certification of Audit of Accounts of PRIs 
(c) Training module of Audit of Gram Panchayats 
(xi) Given the shortage of staff for undertaking formal accounts and 
audit work in the lakhs of Village Panchayats, thousands of 
Intermediate Panchayats and hundreds of Zilla Parishads around 
the country, it is essential that automation and computerization of 
accounts be undertaken with all deliberate speed and to this end 
software like the one beinq prepared by the Xavier Institute of 
Management, Bhubaneshwar for the Orissa State Government, 
for maintaining day-to-day accoun ts, which is expected to be 
ready by early 2004, be deployed as widely as possible 
everywhere. 
(xii) Social audit is an important complement to formal audit and for 
the sound and healthy development of Panchayati Raj, it is 
essential to establish a symbiotic relationship between social and 
formal audit. 
(xiii) Social audit must necessarily be undertaken at the level of the 
Gram Sabha but might also be undertaken at higher levels of the 
Panchayat Raj system, as in West Bengal. 
(xiv) For social audit to be effective and based on the best practices 
available in different States, consideration might be given to the 
preparation of Social Audit Policies for adoption by State 
Legislatures/Governments so as to provide a framework within 
which social audit is undertaken. Such Social Audit Policies may 
be targeted at facilitating popular participation in fighting 
corruption in Panchayats, as also complementing formal audit 
processes by quality assessment, ascertainment of preferences 
and the provision of choices. At the same time, Social Audit 
Policies may provide for institutional measures to prevent 
needless harassment. 
140 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(xv) To ensure appropriate follow-up  to issues raised through social 
audit, legislative bodies and regulatory authorities might treat 
social audit resolutions on par with formal audit paras to ensure 
consideration and disposal within a time-bound frame work. 
(xvi) Given the critical importance of total disclosure of information 
for effective social audit, States  might consider passing Right to 
Information legislation, taki ng into account the legislation 
already on the books in such states as Rajasthan.

accordance with that decision, Public  Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) pay petroleum product's prices on an import parity basis to 
refineries, but full import parity prices are not realized from consumers of 
sensitive products like petrol, diesel, kerosene and domestic LPG. The

between the interests of the stake-holders, namely, consumers, OMCs and the

2308. SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI: Will the Minister of

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR) (a) and (b) Based on the recommendations of 
the Group of Ministers (GoM) the Government have revised the price of 
natural gas with effect from 1.7.2005. 
Effective 1.7.2005, the consumer price of gas produced by ONGC and 
OIL from existing fields given to them on a nomination basis (APM gas) is 
Rs. 3,200 per thousand cubic meter (MCM) exclusive of royalty, taxes & 
levies and transmission charges. 
The power and fertilizer sectors are critical to the economic 
development of the country and the outp ut price of these sectors is either 
controlled for regulated by the Central and State Governments. Therefore, 
these Governments have to bear the burden of large subsidies in these sectors. 
Under court orders, commitments have to be made to specific and users. 
Small scale consumers having allocations upto 0.05 million standard cubic 
meters per day (MMSCMD) are also  given priority in gas supply. 
Accordingly, it has been decided in the public interest, that all available APM 
gas would be supplied to only power and fertilizer sector consumers against 
their existing allocations, in addition to the specific and users committed 
under Court orders and small-scale consumers having allocations upto 0.05 
MMSCMD. However the gas price for transport sector (CNG), Agra 
Ferozabad small industries, and other small scale consumers, with allocations 
upto 0.05 MMSCMD, would be progressively increased over the next 3 to 5 
years to reflect the-market price.

revised to Rs. 1920/MCM effective 1.7.2005.

Study on underground water resources 
2341. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
202 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Central Ground Water Board has found a vast 
subterranean water body of ground water in the belt around the upper Ganga 
canal; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any feasibility study has been conducted to check the 
quantity and quality of this vast underground water resources; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and by when the work in this direction is 
likely to be started? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Based on ground water surveys and exploration carried out by the Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB), an area of 250 sq. km. along Upper Ganga 
Canal has been identified which has potential for development of deeper 
aquifers. The identified area extends from Bhola (North of Jani) in Merrut 
district to Muradnagar in Ghaziabad district in Uttar Pradesh along the Upper 
Ganga Canal. The study has revealed that deeper aquifer between 100 and 
250 m. is unutilized and is separated from top aquifer by a thick clay bed 
varying in thickness from 18 to 55 m. The deeper aquifer is under high 
artesian head and ultimate discharge is in the saline belts in South West. 
(c) and (d) From the studies carried out by CGWB, it has been 
established that quality of deeper aquifer shows deterioration due to base 
exchange from the clay formation. Flow of ground water is very slow and 
over a very long period of time, salinity increases in southward directipn. The 
present quality in identified are is po table and aquifers have high hydraulic 
conductivity with tubewells capable of yielding upto 3000 litres per minute 
(LPM). 
Since the identified area is under the jurisdiction of Government of 
Uttar Pradesh, further action is to be taken by the State Government.

The Supreme Court on 12th August, 2005, through a judgement, allows 
full freedom to the management of t he self-financing private professional 
educational institutions to take all t he students by themselves, denying the 
Government's quota totally. This is against all principles of social justice and, if 
this judgement is implemented, the poor students of all communities will not be 
able to get admission if self-financing educational institutions. The only away 
out from the judgement seems to me is to  have a Central legislation on self-
financing professional educational inst itutions restoring the 50 per cent 
Government quota and making it applicabl e to all self-financed professional 
institutions in the country . And, the fee should be collected as prescribed by 
the Government.

a Bill, in this Session itself, or, immediately take steps to issue an Ordinance 
so that the anxiety of the entire student-community is solved. Thank you.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, no one is  happy that the Bihar Budget is 
being discussed in this House and in the Lok Sabha. Certainly, I am not happy. If 
this situation has come to pass, it is because of the fractur ed mandate delivered 
by the people of Bihar and the inability of  the political parties in Bihar to put 
together a Government. No one in the Central Government can be blamed for 
that. You can blame the Central Government for acting or not acting 
270 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
in a particular manner after a situati on has arisen in Bihar. But that debate 
took place in this House, that debat e has been concluded. It is certainly no 
part of my responsibilities to reopen t hat debate. All I can hope for is the 
passion, the concern and the reason brought to bear on this debate by the 
hon. Members from Bihar should, I hope, help them convince the people of 
Bihar to elect a Government with a work ing majority so that that Government 
can run for five years. 
Sir, the constant refrain has been that money is a problem for Bihar. I 
think, it is time that we laid this ghost to rest. Money has not been a constraint 
in the case of Bihar. Look at the Tw elfth Finance Commission. Bihar will get 
its share of Central taxes, that is a Constitutional mandate and a 
Constitutional provision. No one can deny Bihar one rupee share in the 
Central taxes to which it is  entitled. It is a matter of simple calculation. Let us 
look at grants. The Twelfth Finance Commission has been generous to Bihar. 
There are grants for Panchayati-Raj institutions, grants for urban local bodies, 
grants for calamity relief. Bihar is one among the handful of States chosen by 
the Twelfth Finance Commission for a special grant under education and 
health. 
Under education, while the normal expenditure in five years, beginning 
2005-06 is expected to be about Rs. 20, 410 crores, the grants-in-aid to Bihar 
is Rs. 2,683 crores. Under health, while the normal expenditure for five years 
beginning 2005-06 is Rs. 3,150 crores, the grants-in-aid is Rs. 1,819 crores. 
There are grants for maintenance of forest, there are grants for heritage 
conservation. State-SpecifiQ Need grants for Bihar is Rs. 400 crores. So, I do 
not think money is a constraint. What is a constraint is, I think, better 
administration, better governance, and ac countability for every rupee that is 
spent. 
Sir, in 2005-06 Budget which I pr esent, the outlays have been vastly 
increased over the Revised Estimates of  2004-05. For roads, the increase in 
outlay is 104 per cent, for health it is 45 per cent, for drinking water it is 60 per 
cent, for rural development it is 23.5 per cent, for backward districts 
development under Rashtriya Shram Vikas Yojana it is 205 per cent, for 
urban development it is 104 per cent, fo r irrigation and flood control it is 21.8 
per cent, and agriculture it is 12.5 per cent. 
Power is a constraint. It is true that Bihar has done very poorly so far as 
power is concerned. Bihar's own generation is only about

50 MW. The Central sector allocation to Bihar averages about 700 MW per 
month. The average demand in the St ate is 990 MW and the peak hours 
demand is 1440 MW. Now these four figures give the story of Bihar's power 
sector. National per capita consumption of power is 566 KW/Hours whereas 
Bihar's per capita is only 74 KW/Hours. What I find painful is finger pointing. 
People point fingers to each other. But so meone said that for each finger that 
is pointed, I think, three fingers are pointing to oneself. Everybody has been in 
power in Bihar at some time or the othe r. Bihar's woes did not start in March 
2005; Bihar's woes did not start after President's rule was imposed. Bihar has 
had a history of good governance and poor governance. When Bihar had good 
governance, Bihar was held up as a model for many States. When Bihar had 
poor governance, Bihar and the people of Bihar paid a price. It is not my 
business to fix responsibility. That is the business of the people of Bihar. Nor is 
it my business to find fault. My busi ness is to ensure that the Budget is 
passed, money is provided, and some wo rk is undertaken in the few months 
that we hold responsibility for the Governance of Bihar. Sir, I do not want to go 
into great detail about the numbers; numbers are there in the Budget papers. 
In education, the total outlay in the current year is Rs. 3680 crores. In the 
health sector, the outlay has been increased  from Rs. 783 crores last year to

brought to my notice, I have written to  the Governor pointing out that Plan 
expenditure has been very low, less than five per cent in the first quarter and 
this must be considerably and quickly stepped up. Part of the reason is 
uncertainty that hovers over Bihar and the administration. We were not sure 
whether a Government would be formed;  we were not sure whether the

The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Bill, 2004 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): Sir I 
beg to move: 
That the Bill further to amend the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, be 
taken into consideration. 
Sir, I have the pleasure to commend the Hindu Succession 
(Amendment) Bill, 2004, for consideration of this august House. 
The National Common Minimum Programme of our Government Inter 
alia seeks to give complete legal equality for women in all spheres a practical 
reality, especially by removing discriminative legislation and by enacting a new 
legislation that gives equal rights of ownership of assets like houses and land. 
Sir, you are aware that Article 14 and 15 of our Constitution guarantees 
equality before laws and gender equality. Article 15 of the Convention on the 
Elimination of All forms of Discrim ination Against Women adopted by the 
United Nations General assembly on 18th December, 1979 clearly mandates 
that the State shall accord  to women equality with men before law and in all 
civil matters. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights also guarantees 
substantial equal justice to women. 
Sir, in this perspective, we have brought the Hindu Succession 
(Amendment) Bill, 2004 before this au gust House on 20th December, 2004. 
The Bill was referred to the Parlia mentary Standing Committee, and, I am 
happy to inform this august House that the Committee has returned the Bill 
with certain recommendations. 
Sir, we are all aware that the Hin du law was consolidated in the 50s 
when the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 
1956, the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and the Hindu Minority and 
Guardianship Act, 1956 were adopted. We  generally call these pieces of 
legislations, the Hindu Code as the legislation was originally moved as the 
Hindu code Bill. 
292 

[16 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
After this, there was a demand to confer equality to women in the matter 
of coparcenary property. Section 6 of the Hindu succession Act deals with the 
devolution of interest in coparcenar y property. The provision clearly 
discriminates daughters, as they are not coparceners like the sons. This 
provision has been identified by the La w Commission of India as one of the 
discriminative provisions violating articl es 14 and 15 of the Constitution. The 
Commission made a suo motu study of the discriminative provisions of the 
Hindu Succession Act and presented its 17 4th Report on "Property Rights of 
Women: Proposed reform; under the Hindu Law" (may, 2000) to the Central 
Government. The Government considered the said Report in consultation with 
the State Governments and decided to give  equal right to daughter in Hindu 
joint family property governed by the Mitakshara law. In this connection, I 
would like to inform this august House that several States have already made 
local amendments to the Act. These are:- I) The Hindu Succession (Andhra 
Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986; ii) The Hindu Succession (Tamil Nadu 
Amendment) Act, 1990; iii) The Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) 
Act, 1994; iv) The Hindu Succession (Maharashtra Amendment) Act, 1994; 
and, by the Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1974, the State 
of Kerala has totally abolished the right by birth of males and put an end to the 
joint Hindu family system instead of tinkering with the coparcenary. Sir this has 
to be improved further and now the present law makes certain provisions. The 
benefit of the proposed new secsion relating to devolution of interest in 
coparcenary property is one item, and, declaring daughters also as 
coparceners by birth is proposed to be extended to married daughters as well 
subject to the condition that it shall no t affect or invalidate any disposition or 
alienation including any partition or te stamentary disposition of property which 
has taken place before the introduction of this Bill in Rajya Sabha on 20th 
December, 2004. 
It has been represented that there is a generational difference of depth 
of successors of male and female. It is now proposed fo remove this disparity 
by putting the same depth of a generation in Class One of the heirs. The 
Standing Committee has recommended omi ssion of section 24, which deals 
with prevention of certain widows from inhering property of the interstate if she 
gets remarried as there 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [16 August, 2005] 
is no corresponding disability to widowers. It is proposed to amend this 
section. 
Sir, I think, these are very progressi ve measures and, I hope, there will 
be no difficulty for this hon. House to pass this Bill. With these words, I 
commend this Bill for the consideration of the House. 
The question was proposed.

Inheritance Act 1929, was passed, t hen, in 1937, through Hindu Women's 
Right to Property Act, and then in 1956 and so many amendments to it. But, 
nothing positive has come out. The proposed Bill is, of course, to some extent, 
important towards gender equality and abo lition of the patrilineal system of
